headline: A 2013 House bill that was voted down would have barred people with seriously delinquent federal tax debts from federal jobs.
what_it_does: The bill would have made anyone with a seriously delinquent tax debt ineligible for federal employment or to keep working as a federal employee. A debt counted as seriously delinquent only if a notice of lien had been filed against it in public records. Debts under an approved payment plan or offer in compromise, debts being contested in a collection hearing, debts with a levy issued or agreed to, and debts causing economic hardship would have been exempt. Agencies would have checked public records and asked applicants to certify they had no such debt.

who_it_affects.group: Federal job applicants with a seriously delinquent tax debt
who_it_affects.how: They would have been ineligible for federal jobs unless their debt fell under an exemption.

who_it_affects.group: Current federal employees with a seriously delinquent tax debt
who_it_affects.how: They could have lost their federal jobs unless their debt fell under an exemption.

who_it_affects.group: Federal employees and applicants with tax debts under payment plans or hardship claims
who_it_affects.how: They would have had 180 days to show their debts qualified for an exemption.

who_it_affects.group: Federal agencies and the Office of Personnel Management
who_it_affects.how: Agencies would have had to check public records, collect certifications, and handle tax information, while OPM would have written rules and reported yearly on hardship exemptions.
